planting.note: Divide and replant after flowering into constantly moist, mossy, humus-rich soil on a shaded bank, ideally near a water feature that keeps the roots cool and damp through summer.

directions: Booth's primrose is a petiolarid species from mossy, shaded stream banks of central Nepal through Arunachal Pradesh, where it opens pale lilac to purple flowers with a touch of orange in the throat and a variable white eye in early spring. Because it comes from damp forest banks that sit right above running water, it needs soil that never dries out, paired with bright shade rather than direct sun. Grow it in a cool woodland bed or bog-edge planting with constant leaf-mold moisture, dividing crowded clumps just after bloom to keep them vigorous. It is slower to establish than common primroses and best suited to collectors willing to replicate its wet, shaded native banks.

planting.note: Grow in deep or partial shade in a gritty, humus-rich mix under glass, in an alpine house pan, or in a sheltered rock crevice, keeping winter moisture to a minimum.

directions: Native to steep, rocky Nepalese cliff faces at 3600 to 4300 meters, this miniature primrose carries spoon-shaped leaves dusted white with farina and rimmed with fine teeth, topped by umbels of creamy white to soft yellow flowers with a deeper golden eye. Its vertical rock-face habitat means it tolerates far more shade than most alpines but demands sharp drainage, since its chief enemy is winter wet rather than cold itself. Alpine growers typically keep it in a clay pan under glass or in a sheltered crevice bed where humidity can be controlled by hand rather than left to the weather. Avoid any mix that stays soggy after rain, and resist overwatering during its winter rest.

planting.note: Plant divisions in a lime-free, gritty scree mix in a trough or rockery crevice with light afternoon shade; keep roots cool and evenly moist through the growing season.

directions: A compact, cushion-forming primrose of the Pyrenees and Alps, this species produces toothed, pale green rosettes and flat-faced flowers that range from pale pink through deep cerise-mauve to white, each with a contrasting pale eye, opening on wet cliff ledges and grassy alpine slopes. Unlike many petiolarid primroses it tolerates more light and is usually grown in a partly shaded rock garden crevice or raised trough rather than deep woodland shade. Because the species is calcifuge, avoid limestone grit and instead use a lime-free, humus-rich scree mix that still drains sharply after rain. It is one of the parent species behind the long line of garden Auricula hybrids and stays under 6 inches tall even at full size.

planting.note: Divide and replant after flowering into cool, humus-rich, constantly moist soil in deep shade, mimicking the montane forest floor of its native Himalayan range.

directions: Found from Bhutan and northeast India to Nepal and Sikkim at mid elevation, this petiolarid primrose takes its common name from the pinkish-lilac flowers that each show a bright orange-yellow throat, carried in clusters above a bell-shaped, white-farinose calyx. The whole flowering stem is powdered white like the sepals, giving the inflorescence a frosted look against the clear-colored petals. It wants the same cool, constantly damp, humus-rich forest-floor conditions as its Petiolares relatives, and resents both summer drought and direct sun. Best grown in a shaded woodland bed or raised trough where leaf litter can be renewed each year to hold moisture around the crown.

planting.note: Grow in deep shade in constantly moist, humus-rich soil near a stream bank or in a sheltered woodland bed; protect from direct sun and hard freezes.

directions: Close kin to Primula gracilipes, this East Nepal to west Bhutan species grows on wet forest banks and spray-soaked ground beside streams and waterfalls, producing crowded umbels of a dozen or more bright pink flowers with a white-ringed yellow eye held low among the yellow-farinose leaves. Its flowering stems are so short the blooms rest almost directly on the foliage rather than rising above it, a trait distinctive enough to have earned the species its name. It is noticeably less cold-hardy than most Petiolares primroses and dislikes any direct sun, doing best in a consistently damp, shaded woodland or bog-edge planting. Vigorous once established, it can be short-lived in cultivation and benefits from regular propagation by division to guard against loss.
